chapters.title: The Arrow of Fire
paragraphs: Byomkesh sat up with a start and said, "Do you know how much it costs to go to Kashmir?"
"How much?"
"At least a thousand rupees. Where would I get that kind of money?"
Satyabati, her temper flaring, stood up and said, "I don’t know about all that. Just tell me if you’ll go or not."
"I told you, I don’t have the money."

At that moment, there was a knock at the outer door. What promised to be a most enjoyable marital quarrel was thus abruptly interrupted. Satyabati, having scorched Byomkesh with a few sharp, half-spoken barbs, retreated into the inner rooms.

I lit the lamp and opened the door. The man standing outside appeared, at first glance, to be little more than a youth. Not very tall, slim and wiry, with a fair, handsome face marked by the faintest trace of a moustache. His attire was immaculate, from the deerskin shoes on his feet to the sheer muslin panjabi draped over his frame—everything about him was impeccable.
"Whom do you seek?"
"The satyanweshi, Byomkesh Babu."
"Come in," I said, stepping aside from the door.

The man entered and stood beneath the bright electric light, allowing me a better look at his features. Not as young as I had first thought; there was a subtle ripeness to his complexion. His eyes bore the imprint of worldly experience, with fine shadows etched at their corners, and beneath the outward delicacy of his face, the bones had already begun to harden with age. Yet he could not have been more than twenty-five.
Byomkesh, who had been observing the visitor from beside the takhtposh, now rose and took a seat in a chair. Indicating the chair opposite, he said, "Sit. What brings you to me?"
The man did not answer at once. He sat down, studied us both with careful attention for a moment, and then said, "You’ll do for my purpose."
Byomkesh raised his brows. "Is that so? And what is this purpose?"

The young man drew a bundle of notes from his side pocket and, with an air of indifference, tossed them onto the table before Byomkesh. "If I should die suddenly, you are to investigate the cause of my death. That is the task. Since I may not be able to pay you later, I am giving you your fee in advance. Count it—one thousand rupees."

Byomkesh gazed at the youth with narrowed eyes for a moment, then counted the bundle. Ten crisp notes of one hundred rupees each. Setting the notes to one side of the table, Byomkesh lazily glanced at me; a glimmer of amusement flickered in his eyes. Then, fixing a grave look upon the young man’s face, he said, "I have a few questions for you. Whether I accept your case will depend on your answers."

The youth opened a gold cigarette case and offered it to Byomkesh, who shook his head in refusal. Lighting a cigarette for himself, the young man exhaled a plume of smoke and said, "Ask. But I may not answer every question."
Byomkesh was silent for a moment, then asked in a languid tone, "What is your name?"
A quick smile played across the young man’s lips—a rather captivating smile. He replied, "I haven’t told you that yet. My name is Satyakam Das."
"Satyakam?"
"Yes! Just as you are a satyanweshi, I am Satyakam."
Byomkesh Samagra

“I haven’t heard this name before. Satyakam—is that an alias?” “No, it’s my real name.” “Hm. Where do you live? What’s your address?” “I live in Calcutta. 33/34 Amherst Street.” “What do you do?” “Work? I don’t do anything in particular. Have you heard of Suchitra Emporium, of Das-Chowdhury Company?” “I have. The large jewelry store on Dharmatala Street.” “I’m a partner at Suchitra Emporium.” “A partner. —Who are the other partners?” Satyakam drew a breath and said, “My father—Ushapati Das.” Byomkesh looked at him with a questioning gaze. Satyakam hesitated for a moment, then, reluctantly, he said, “My maternal grandfather founded Suchitra Emporium. Later, my father became his partner. Now Grandfather has passed away, and he left his share to me. My mother was his only child. I am my mother’s only child.” “I see.” Byomkesh seemed lost in thought for a moment, then asked in a detached tone, “Do you drink?” Without the least embarrassment, Satyakam replied, “I do. You caught the scent, didn’t you?” “How old are you?” “I’m twenty-one. Want to know my birth date? July 7, 1927.” Satyakam smiled with a hint of irony. “How long have you been drinking?” “I started at fourteen.” Satyakam lit a fresh cigarette from the stub of the last. “Do you drink all the time?” “Whenever I feel like it.” With that, he took a four-ounce flask from his pocket and showed it. Byomkesh sat for a while, his hand on his cheek. I, too, gazed in silence at this twenty-one-year-old youth. Those who wish to conquer the three worlds by casting off all shame must, I suppose, begin their training at a very early age. Byomkesh raised his head and, in the same impassive tone, asked, “Do you have other vices as well?” Satyakam smirked, “Why call them vices, Byomkesh-babu? Can something so universal truly be a vice?” My skin crawled. Byomkesh, however, replied with an unruffled face, “Let’s leave the philosophical debate aside. Have you set your sights on respectable women as well?” “I have.” There was a distinct note of satisfaction in Satyakam’s voice. “How many women have you ruined?” “I haven’t kept count, Byomkesh-babu.” Satyakam grinned shamelessly. Byomkesh made a gesture of distaste. “You say you might die suddenly. Is it your fear that someone will murder you?” “Yes.” “Who might want to kill you? The relatives of the women you’ve harmed? Do you suspect anyone?”
Rokter Daag 563

“Do you suspect anyone?” “I do. But I won’t name names.” “You won’t even try to save your own life?” Satyakam’s face twisted into a desolate expression as he made to rise. “There’s no use trying, Byomkesh-babu. Well, I’ll take your leave now, I suppose you have no more questions. I have an appointment tonight.” That this appointment was not of a business nature was evident from the sly smile that played on his lips. As he reached the door, Byomkesh called after him, “If someone murders you, how will I know?” Satyakam turned and replied, “You’ll read about it in the papers. Besides, you can always make inquiries. I doubt you’ll have to wait long.” Once Satyakam had departed, I closed the door and sank down onto the divan. Satyabati re-entered, her face alight with laughter. It seemed she had been waiting just outside the door. “You were worrying about that thousand rupees, and now you’ve got it!” Byomkesh, with a sour face, handed the notes towards Satyabati and said, “The ant eats sugar, Chintamani supplies it. Well, what else—start making arrangements for our trip to Kashmir.” He turned to me. “Well, what did you make of the lad?” I said, “I’ve never seen such a brazen, two-faced scoundrel at such a young age.” Byomkesh said, “Nor have I. But it’s strange—he doesn’t want to save his own life, but he wants an investigation after his death!”
Two

The next morning, Satyabati said, “If we’re going to Kashmir, where are the quilts and bedding?” Byomkesh replied, “Why, didn’t we have them last year in Patna?” Satyabati said, “Those all belong to your elder brothers. Do we have anything of our own? The mild winters of Calcutta are manageable, but for Kashmir, we’ll need at least two English blankets and a beaver coat for me.” “Hm. Come on, Ajit, let’s go out.” I asked, “Where are we going?” He said, “Let’s go to Suchitra Emporium. We’ll kill two birds with one stone.” I said, “Why not take Satyabati along? She can choose her own things.” Byomkesh glanced at Satyabati. In a plaintive voice, she said, “I’d love to go, but how can I? The school car will be coming for Khoka.” Byomkesh said, “You don’t need to come. I’ll pick out your things myself. Don’t worry, you won’t be disappointed.” Satyabati cast a laughing, sidelong glance at Byomkesh as she went inside, her unwavering faith in his taste evident. In truth, I had always done the shopping for Satyabati’s fashionable things. But now spring had arrived, the month of Phalgun was passing— The two of us set out. By half past nine, we reached Dharmatala Street and saw that the emporium’s...

The door stood open, the heavy curtains drawn aside from the immense glass windows. We stepped inside. It was a vast room, its mosaic floor dotted here and there with showcases displaying an array of elegant wares. A handful of customers, most of them upper-class ladies, had already arrived and were browsing. The staff stood at their stations, attending to the whims of the clientele. A distinguished elderly gentleman paced from one end of the room to the other, his watchful gaze sweeping over everything.
As we entered, the elderly gentleman approached and greeted us with respectful courtesy. “Please, come in. What may I show you?”
Byomkesh glanced about the room, his voice hesitant. “Just a small thing—two British blankets. Would you have them?”
“Certainly. This way, please.” The gentleman led us aside. “Anything else?”
“And a ladies’ beaver coat.”
“You’ll find both. Here’s the lift—upstairs you’ll get blankets and beaver coats alike.”
In the corner of the room, a small lift was ascending and descending. As we moved to stand before it, a voice called from behind, “I’ll take care of these gentlemen.”

Turning at the familiar voice, we saw Satyakam. Dressed in a silk suit, his appearance was neat and trim—he must have been in this very room all along, but his foreign attire had made him unremarkable to us until now. The elderly gentleman, seeing him, said, “Ah—very well. Take them upstairs, they want to buy British blankets and a beaver coat.” With a brief smile in our direction, he moved off elsewhere.
Byomkesh glanced quickly from Satyakam to the elderly gentleman, and asked softly, “Is he your—?”
Satyakam suppressed a smile. “Partner.”
“In other words—your father!”
Satyakam nodded in assent.

Though I had seen the elderly gentleman before, I had not truly observed him until now. He stood a little distance away, conversing with another customer, yet every so often, his gaze flickered uneasily in our direction. He was a tall, broad-shouldered man of dusky complexion, his jawline firm and pronounced. He looked to be about forty-five, with a touch of grey at his temples. Despite the practiced courtesy of a shopkeeper, there was an ascetic harshness about his face—a certain austerity. I suspected that, beneath the veneer of business, his temperament was rather stern.
At that moment, the lift descended. We stepped into its cage and arrived at the second floor.
Satyakam arched his brows at Byomkesh with a playful gesture. “Are you really here to buy something? Or is this a field investigation?”
“I intend to buy.”

The upper floor was not arranged like the one below; it resembled a storeroom more than a showroom. Yet even here, a few customers wandered about. Satyakam led us to the section for warm clothing. At his signal, an attendant brought out a variety of British blankets for our inspection. Byomkesh, in matters such as these, could hardly tell the difference between chintz and chintamani; it was left to me to select two blankets. The price was steep, but the quality was excellent.
Next, the beaver coats. Coats of every color and size—all of them exorbitantly priced. As we examined them, Satyakam remarked, “Are you thinking about the size?”
Rokter Dag 565
A beaver coat can be a little loose, it doesn’t matter. Take whichever you like, and if it’s completely unsuitable, I’ll exchange it for you.’

I was drawn to a deep purple coat, but hesitated when I saw the price tag. Satyakam, sensing my predicament, said, ‘Don’t worry about the price. That’s for regular customers. You’ll get it at the purchase price. —Come.’
He led us to the cashier and said, ‘These items are to be given at the purchase rate. Please make out the cash memo.’

‘As you wish,’ said the elderly cashier, writing out the memo. I noticed the price was nearly fifty rupees less than the tag. My spirits lifted; the impression I’d formed of Satyakam last night shifted considerably. No, whatever else he may be, the fellow is not a complete bloodsucker.

At that moment, a young woman appeared on the upper floor. Fair-skinned, youthful, her attire and manner spoke of a life of indulgence and refinement. Satyakam turned his head once to glance at her; his expression changed. With one eye narrowed, he said to us, ‘I suppose you don’t have anything else to buy? In that case—I have a new customer—well then, goodbye.’

Like a bee drawn to the scent of honey, Satyakam flew straight toward the young woman. By the time we had our purchases packed and were about to descend, we saw that Satyakam had thoroughly enchanted her; the young woman, drinking in his every word, followed him wherever he led.
Back at home, we showed Satyabati our purchases. She was utterly delighted and heaped all the praise for our discerning choices upon Byomkesh. Such is the glory of spring!
When I mentioned the reduction in price, Satyabati exclaimed in surprise, ‘Really? What a nice boy Satyakam is!’
Byomkesh exhaled a plume of smoke toward the ceiling and said, ‘A very nice boy! A golden boy! If no one murders him, his shop will be bankrupt soon enough.’
In the evening, Byomkesh took me out for a walk. This time our path led toward Amherst Street. By the time we reached house number 33/34, dusk had fallen thick and heavy.

At this hour of twilight, even the footpaths of Calcutta grow deserted for a brief spell, perhaps waiting for the streetlights to flicker on. We stopped in front of our destination. There were few passersby, only a man wrapped in a shawl pacing the pavement, who moved a little distance away when he saw us.

House number 33/34 did not stand flush with the footpath. First, a small iron gate, then a narrow brick-paved lane like an alley, running twenty or twenty-five feet up to the main entrance. A two-storied house, not very large from the front. On either side of the main door were two windows, and above them on the first floor, two round balconies. No lights were yet burning inside. Standing on the pavement, I thought I saw a woman sitting in one of the upstairs balconies, reading a book or perhaps sewing. Through the wrought-iron railing of the balcony, I caught a faint glimpse.
‘Byomkesh-babu!’
At the sudden call from behind, we both turned. The man we’d seen pacing the pavement, wrapped in his shawl, had come up behind us. A well-built young man,
Byomkesh Samagra

His hair was cropped short, and his face seemed oddly familiar. Byomkesh asked, “Who are you?” The young man replied, “Don’t you recognize me, sir? I came the other day to collect a subscription for Saraswati Puja. My name is Nanda Ghosh, I live in your para.” Byomkesh said, “Ah, now I remember. But you’re from the other side of the neighborhood—what brings you here, wandering about at this hour of the evening?” “Sir—” One of Nanda Ghosh’s hands slipped out from under his shawl and just as quickly disappeared back inside. Still, I caught a glimpse of it—a vindipal, a heavy iron knuckle-duster. Though small in size, in the hands of a strong man it could be a deadly weapon. Byomkesh eyed Nanda Ghosh with suspicion and said, “What’s your game? Out with it.” “My game—sir—” Nanda edged closer and lowered his voice, “I’ll tell you, sir. There’s a fellow living in this house—I’ve come to thrash him.” “Is that so! And why do you want to thrash him?” “There’s a reason, sir. But what are you doing here? Do you know someone in this house?” “I know Satyakam. He’s the one you want to thrash, isn’t it?” “Sir—” Nanda seemed a little unsettled. “Are you very close to him?” “No, not close. But I’d like to know why you want to beat him up. Has he wronged you in some way?” “Wronged—well, that’s a long story, sir. If you want to hear it, come with me. Bhuteshwar’s akhra is nearby, I’ll tell you everything there.” “Bhuteshwar’s akhra?” “Yes, sir, our wrestling club. It’s just down the lane. Come.” “Let’s go.” By now, the streetlights had come on. We followed Nanda into a narrow alley, and after a short walk, arrived at a walled courtyard. Beside the courtyard stood a couple of damp, crumbling rooms, their windows glowing with light. The yard itself was almost dark; a few bare-chested youths were doing push-ups, swinging mughurs, and otherwise hardening their bodies in various ways. Nanda led us past them and into one of the rooms. A satranji was spread on the floor; an enormous man sat there. Nanda introduced him: this was the wrestling club’s ustad, Bhuteshwar Bag. The name suited him—his skin was ghostly pale, his face tiger-like, and his body as massive as an elephant’s. Not a single hair on his head; he must have been close to sixty. Perhaps in his youth he’d been a goonda or a wrestler, but now, in old age, he ran this gymnasium. Nanda said, “Bhuteshwarda, this is Byomkesh Babu, a famous detective. He knows Satyakam.” Bhuteshwar turned his tigerish eyes on Byomkesh and asked, “Are you with the police? That boy’s guardian?” Byomkesh politely explained that he was not with the police, and had only met Satyakam once. He simply wanted to know why there was a need to beat Satyakam—he had no other motive. Bhuteshwar softened a little and said, “That boy’s a real scoundrel. Some of the gentlemen in our para have complained to us. He harasses the girls. This is a respectable neighborhood—we won’t tolerate such things here.” At that moment, a few more burly wrestlers entered the room and sat down around us.
The Bloodstain 567

He scrutinized us with a hard, unblinking stare. It was clear as daylight that the plan to thrash Satyakam was not the whim of a single man; the entire gymnasium committee had sanctioned it. A chill of unease crept over me regarding our own safety. The situation was precarious—Satyakam’s trap might well snap shut upon us instead.

Byomkesh, however, kept his composure. In a calm voice, he said, “If someone from the para misbehaves, it is the duty of the people of the para to discipline him. Such matters cannot be settled by outsiders. I have no objection if you wish to teach Satyakam a lesson. From what I know of him, a couple of blows across his back might do him some good. Only one thing—don’t go so far as murder! And, do it carefully, so that you don’t get caught.”

Nanda grinned and said, “That’s exactly why I’ve taken the job upon myself, sir. I’ll give him a few knocks and slip away. I’m not from this para— even if they recognize me, they won’t be able to identify me.”
Byomkesh smiled and rose to his feet. “Still, if any trouble arises, let me know. We’ll take our leave now. Namaskar, Bhuteshwar-babu.”
Nanda escorted us to the main road and then returned to the akhra. Byomkesh exhaled deeply and said, “My word, we really stuck our necks into the tiger’s den!”
I said, “But was it right of you to encourage them to beat up Satyakam? You’ve taken his money.”
Byomkesh replied, “If a few blows can save his life, isn’t that better?”
Three
Though I have never worked in an office in my life, for some reason I always wake late on Sunday mornings. My ancestors were government clerks, perhaps the stain of servitude lingers in my blood.

The next day was Sunday. At half past seven, rubbing the sleep from my eyes, I entered the outer room to find Byomkesh holding the newspaper wide open in both hands, staring at it intently. He didn’t turn his gaze at my arrival; it was as if he addressed the newspaper itself, reciting, “O messenger, your tidings are like the dreams of night!”
His demeanor struck me as odd. I asked, “What’s happened?”
He lowered the paper and said, “Satyakam died last night.”
“What! How did he die?”
“I don’t know. Get ready—we have to leave within half an hour.”
I picked up the newspaper. At the bottom of the middle page, a five-line report—
—In the small hours of this morning, Satyakam Das, the well-known proprietor of Suchitra Emporium, Dharmatala, has died under suspicious circumstances. Police have taken up the investigation.
So Satyakam had sensed it—he had foreseen his death. But so soon! The first thing that came to mind was Nanda Ghosh, skulking in the shadows beneath his shawl outside the house last evening—
At half past eight, Byomkesh and I arrived at Amherst Street. A constable stood on the pavement outside the gate; after a bit of scrutiny, he allowed us to enter.
Byomkesh Samagra

We arrived at the main entrance by way of the brick-paved road. The front door stood open, but there was no one in sight. Nor was there any sound of weeping or lamentation from inside the house. Byomkesh, upon reaching the doorway, halted abruptly and silently pointed to the ground. I saw that, right in front of the door where the brick path ended, there was a stain of blood. Not fresh blood, but a patch the size of a palm, dried and caked into a dark crust.
We exchanged a glance; Byomkesh nodded. Skirting the bloodstained spot, we entered the house.

A wide veranda stretched before us, with two doors on either side. One was locked, the other open; through the open door, a medium-sized office room was visible. In the center of the room stood a large table, and facing it, Ushapati Babu sat alone.
Ushapati Babu sat with both elbows resting on the table, his chin cupped in his palms. As we entered, he raised his sorrow-filled eyes to us and, in a dry, weary voice, asked, “What do you want?”
Byomkesh stepped up to the table and, in a tone of sympathy, said, “Forgive me for disturbing you at such a time. My name is Byomkesh Bakshi—”
Ushapati Babu, becoming slightly more alert, turned his gaze from one to the other, then said, “I’ve seen you somewhere before. Perhaps at Suchitra’s. —What did you say your name was?”
“Byomkesh Bakshi. This is Ajit Bandyopadhyay. —Yesterday we visited your shop—”

It did not seem that Ushapati Babu remembered our names from before, but the natural courtesy of a shopkeeper toward a customer appeared ingrained in his very bones; so, without displaying any impatience, he said, “Is there something you need? I’m a bit—there’s been an accident at home—”
Byomkesh said, “I know. That’s why we’ve come. Satyakam Babu—”
“You knew Satyakam?”
“I met him only the day before yesterday. He came to me with a proposal—”
“What proposal?”
“He proposed that, should he die suddenly, I would investigate the circumstances of his death.”

Ushapati Babu now sat up straight, staring at us for a moment with unblinking eyes, as if suppressing a surge of emotion. Then, in a controlled voice, he said, “Please, have a seat. —So Satyakam understood, after all. But forgive me, I don’t understand why Satyakam came to you. You—your identity—are you with the police? But the police were here last night, they—”
“No, I am not with the police. I am a satyanweshi—a seeker of truth. You could say a private detective.”
“Oh—” Ushapati Babu was silent for a long while, then said, “Did Satyakam tell you whom he suspected?”
“No, he mentioned no names. —If you permit, I would like to investigate.”
“But—the police have already taken charge of the investigation. What more could you do?”
“I don’t know yet if I can do anything at all, but I can try.”
Rokter Daag 569
Even in the midst of such overwhelming grief, Ushapati Babu had not lost his presence of mind—this became clear to me now.
He said, "You are a private detective. How much must I pay you for your services?"
Byomkesh replied, "You need not pay me anything. My fee has already been settled by Satyakam Babu."
Ushapati Babu fixed Byomkesh with a sharp gaze, then lowered his eyes and murmured, "Oh. Well, investigate if you must. But there is no use, Byomkesh Babu."
"No use? Why not?"
"Satyakam will not return, will he? What is the point of muddying the waters?"
Byomkesh regarded Ushapati Babu with steady eyes for a moment, then spoke in a calm voice, "I understand your feelings. Rest assured, I will not stir up trouble. My only aim is to uncover the truth."
Ushapati Babu let out a weary sigh. "Very well. Tell me what I must do."
Byomkesh said, "I know nothing of how or when Satyakam Babu died last night. Can you tell me?"

Ushapati Babu’s face grew even more drawn. He ran a hand across his chest and said, "Who else is there to tell you but me? Last night, at one o’clock, I was asleep in my own room when a sound woke me. A sudden, sharp noise. It seemed to come from the direction of the main entrance—"
"Forgive me, where is your bedroom?"
Ushapati Babu pointed upward toward the ceiling. "The room above this one. I sleep alone; my wife sleeps in the adjoining room."
"And which room did Satyakam Babu sleep in?"
"Satyakam slept downstairs. That room across the verandah, the one with the locked door—that was his. My wife’s bedroom is directly above his."
"Why did Satyakam Babu sleep downstairs?"

Ushapati Babu did not answer. He gazed absently out the window. From his manner, it was clear that Satyakam slept downstairs for the convenience of coming and going at night without disturbance. There was no fixed hour for his return home.

At that moment, the curtain over the inner doorway was drawn aside and a young woman entered, carrying a glass of sherbet. She stopped short at the sight of us, hesitated, and in an uncertain voice said, "Mama—" but then stood rooted to the spot, silent. The girl was seventeen or eighteen, not beautiful, but well-formed and lively. At present, a shadow of anxiety darkened her face and eyes.
Ushapati Babu turned to her and said, "No need." The girl withdrew.
Byomkesh asked, "Who else lives in your house?"
Ushapati Babu replied, "Besides us, my nephew and niece live here."
"That was your niece?"
"Yes."
"How long have they been with you?"
"Their father died about a year ago. Their mother passed away before that. Since then, I have been their guardian. Apart from us, there is no one else in the house."
"Servants?"
Byomkesh Samagra
“The old servant, Sahadev, lives in the house. Besides him, there’s a maid and a cook, but they don’t stay at night.”
“I see. Now, tell me about last night’s events.”

Mr. Ushapati ran his palm over his eyes once and said, “Yes. Hearing the noise, I opened the balcony door and stepped outside. It was pitch dark below; I couldn’t see a thing. Then, from near the main door, Sahadev suddenly screamed… I rushed down, and saw Sahadev had opened the door, and—Satyakam was lying in front of it. Lifeless, a bullet had entered from his back.”
“A bullet! From a gun?”

“Yes. Satyakam would return home late every night. Sahadev used to sleep on the veranda, and whenever he heard a knock, he’d get up and open the door. Last night, before he could open it after hearing the knock, someone shot Satyakam from behind.”
“A bullet. I had thought—” Byomkesh paused, then said, “Go on.”
Mr. Ushapati let out a stifled sigh. “What else? I telephoned the police.”
Byomkesh sat for a while, head bowed in thought. Then he looked up and asked, “Who locked Satyakam’s room?”
Ushapati replied, “Whenever Satyakam left the house, he’d lock his room. I believe he did so yesterday as well, and then—”
“I understand. So the room key is with the police?”
“Most likely.”
“The police haven’t opened the room?”
“No.”
“Well, I have nothing more to ask you for now. I’d like to speak to the other members of the household.”
“Tell me whom to call.”
“Is Sahadev in the house?”
“Of course. I’ll call him.”
Mr. Ushapati rose and called Sahadev from near the inner doorway, then returned and sat down.

Sahadev entered. A decrepit old man, little more than skin and bones. A wild shock of white hair on his head, white brows, even the pupils of his eyes had turned pale. Loose skin, slack muscles, and a vacant, almost simple-minded look on his face.
Byomkesh asked, “Your name is Sahadev? How many years have you worked in this house?”
Sahadev did not reply. He stared blankly, first at us, then at Mr. Ushapati. Ushapati said, “He’s been here since my father-in-law’s time—almost thirty-five years.”
Byomkesh turned to Sahadev. “Last night, you—”
Before Byomkesh could finish, Sahadev folded his hands and said, “I know nothing, babu.”
Byomkesh said, “Listen to my question and answer. Last night, when Satyakam-babu knocked at the door, were you awake?”
Rokter Daag 571
Sahadev, as before, spoke with folded hands, “I don’t know anything, babu.”
Byomkesh pierced him with a sharp gaze and said, “Try to remember. Did you hear any sudden noise at that time?”
“I don’t know anything, babu.”

No matter how many questions Byomkesh asked thereafter, Sahadev gave only one answer—“I don’t know anything, babu.” How much truth lay in this all-encompassing ignorance was hard to guess; in short, even if Sahadev did know something, he would not say it. Byomkesh, growing irritated, said, “You may go. Ushapati-babu, please call your niece now.”
Ushapati-babu said to Sahadev, “Go call Chumki.”

Sahadev left. A short while later, Chumki entered, and with a deliberate firmness, came to stand beside the table. I saw that the shadow of anxiety on her face had deepened; she raised her eyes towards us only to lower them again at once.
Byomkesh spoke in an easy tone, “I hear from your uncle that you have been living in this house for about a year now. Where did you live before?”

Outwardly, he was an impeccably polished young man, but inside, he was cunning and consumed by jealousy. His behavior toward Ushapati and Suchitra grew increasingly vicious. One day, he said bluntly to his mother, “With what right do you try to discipline me? I know everything.” To Ushapati he said, “You are not my father—why should I show you any respect?”

Life in the house became unbearable for Ushapati and Suchitra. Meanwhile, at the shop, Satyakam began to play a different game. Now he was a partner in the business, with rights equal to Ushapati’s. He began to exercise those rights to the fullest. In a refined shop like Suchitra’s, there were always more female customers than male; Satyakam would pick out the young and beautiful among them, strike up friendships, sell them expensive goods at a discount, and take them out to dine at hotels. He would withdraw as much money as he pleased from the shop’s funds and squander it with both hands. Drinking, horse racing, gambling at the city’s grandest clubs—these became his daily pursuits.

Within a year of Ramakanta’s death, it became clear that the shop was in trouble; it could not go on like this much longer. When Ushapati Babu tried to intervene, Satyakam retorted, “I’m spending my own money—what’s it to you?” Worse, a rumor began to circulate that it was not safe for women to visit their shop. Customers dwindled. Distraught, Ushapati Babu had no idea what to do.

When the situation had become utterly dire, an incident occurred. One evening, Ushapati returned home for some reason. As he was about to enter his room upstairs, he heard a muffled, anguished moan coming from the adjoining room—his wife’s chamber. Stepping softly, Ushapati approached the door. He saw his wife alone on the floor, banging her head and crying, “Is my atonement still not over? I can’t bear it any longer!”

Ushapati slipped quietly downstairs. Asking Sahadev, he learned that earlier that evening, an elderly lady from the para had come by and heaped insults on Suchitra. Apparently, Satyakam had been taking the woman’s daughter to the cinema and treating her to meals at fancy hotels.
That very day, Ushapati resolved that Satyakam must be removed. Unless he killed him, there would be no escape from any direction. Life could not go on like this.

Ushapati began to prepare. He had one advantage: if Satyakam were murdered, no one would suspect him. To the outside world, Satyakam was his son—no one would believe a father could kill his own child. Satyakam had many enemies; suspicion would fall on them.
